subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Britain's Tea Obsession
description: Learn Britain's Tea Obsession in one minute.

hook.text: By 1800, Britain was importing 24 million pounds of tea per year. The nation was addicted.

buildup.text: Tea crossed class lines. Workers drank it with sugar for quick energy; elites took it with ceremony.

discovery.text: The British added milk to their tea, partly because cheap porcelain cracked from hot liquid alone.

twist.text: Smuggling supplied nearly two-thirds of Britain's tea by 1780—taxes made legal tea absurdly expensive.

climax.text: Prime Minister William Pitt slashed the tea tax in 1784, killing the smuggling trade overnight.

punchline.text: Smugglers, taxes, milk, and sugar. Britain built an identity.

quiz.question: Why was tea smuggling so common in 18th-century Britain?
options: High taxes made legal tea extremely expensive

details.summary: By the 1700s, Britain had become the world's most tea-obsessed nation. The East India Company imported massive quantities, sugar sweetened it for working-class palates, and tea became the national drink. It fueled workers, structured the day, and defined British social rituals for centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Britain's tea obsession shaped global trade, colonial policy, and geopolitics. Tea was not just a drink but a force that influenced wars, economies, and empires.
takeaways: Tea became Britain's national drink by the 1700s
The East India Company controlled the massive import trade
Sugar and milk made tea palatable to all social classes

faq.question: How much tea did Britain consume at its peak?
faq.answer: By the mid-1800s, Britain imported over 30 million kilograms of tea annually. Per capita consumption was the highest in the world. Workers drank tea multiple times a day. It was added to rations for soldiers, sailors, and factory workers as an essential rather than a luxury.

faq.question: Why did the British add milk and sugar to tea?
faq.answer: Sugar, cheaply available from Caribbean plantations, masked the bitterness of lower-quality tea. Milk may have been added to protect delicate porcelain cups from hot liquid. The combination made tea more caloric and palatable for workers who needed cheap energy.
